title: Marches and the school band at military school
summary: Jones marched to records as a small boy and learned trumpet at military school playing Sousa and color-book marches.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Do you remember the first march you ever learned? How about you?

As a very little boy, my mother would take me to my grandmother's house. She had a wind up Vic Troller. And she had a bunch of march records. She would show me how to operate it. And I'd wind it up, crank it up, put the record on, and march around the room to probably Stars and Stripes Forever or one of those marches, by whom I don't know.
And would you play the banjo?
No. That was even before that, as a little, maybe three or four year old boy.
Oh, yeah. And did you play marches on the trumpet when you battled that?
When I first started playing, that was all I did play, because I was at a military school in the school band. And I learned how to play the instrument to play marches.
Yeah. And what did you play? Do you remember the marches there?

We did a lot of Susan marches. And there are some standard marches that even today, I notice that are very popular amongst high school bands. You'll hear them playing in a Rose Bowl parade or things like that, or see them in parades in the street. I don't remember the names of the book. We always refer to them by the color of the book. It was the red book or the blue book or the green book. And number, so and so march in the red book. I don't know. And they all had very common names and were fairly easy to play, very forgettable melody lines. And then we had some of the Susan marches that were very difficult for a 35 piece high school marching band to play, these grand arrangements.
But they were forgettable, you say? Most of the other ones, yeah.
Yes, they were. Yes, they were.
